subject: Career
title: Finding Your Unique Value Proposition
description: Learn Finding Your Unique Value Proposition in one minute.

hook.text: There are millions of marketers, engineers, and designers. Why should someone pick you?

buildup.text: Your unique value proposition sits at the intersection of skills, passion, and market need.

discovery.text: It's not about being the best at one thing. It's about a rare combination nobody else has.

twist.text: Scott Adams calls this the 'talent stack' — be top 25% in three things, not top 1% in one.

climax.text: Map your skills: what do you do that others find hard, enjoy, and that people pay for?

punchline.text: You don't need to be the best. You need to be the only.

quiz.question: What is Scott Adams' 'talent stack' concept?
options: Be top 25% in multiple skills instead of top 1% in one

details.summary: Your unique value proposition is the specific combination of skills, experiences, and perspectives that only you offer. In a competitive job market, differentiation comes not from being the best at one thing but from having an unreplicable combination.
details.whyItMatters: Competing on a single skill means fighting everyone in that category. A unique combination creates a niche where you face little competition and command premium value.
takeaways: Combine two or three distinct skills for a unique positioning
Your unusual background or hobby may be your strongest differentiator
Test your value proposition by checking if others can claim the same thing

faq.question: How do you identify your unique value proposition if you feel average?
faq.answer: List your top three skills, your unusual life experiences, and what people consistently ask your help with. The intersection of these reveals uniqueness that feels ordinary to you but rare to the market. Others' shock at your abilities often points to your differentiator.

faq.question: Can your unique value proposition change over time as your career evolves?
faq.answer: Absolutely. Your value proposition should evolve as you gain new skills and experiences. The core differentiator often remains stable, but the way you frame and apply it shifts with career stages and market conditions.
